summary:
Libya's Penal Code penalises "illicit sexual intercourse" and "indecent acts", with the indecent-acts provisions carrying up to five years' imprisonment. Same-sex relations are not legal for men or women. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records the position plainly, and The Guardian's regional guide lists Libya among states where imprisonment is the penalty for homosexuality, noting that where no specific law exists other laws are used and that terms vary from country to country.

Cairo 52's country review finds de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process itself, whether social, medical or surgical, enforced through those same indecent-acts and illicit-intercourse provisions. Recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible, which narrows the ground on which a trans person can seek care or be seen in public.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: official identity documents cannot be changed. Same-sex relationships are not legally recognised, no legal protections exist against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Violence against people suspected of same-sex relations or gender nonconformity has been documented at the hands of militias as well as armed extremist groups. In November 2012 a Libyan militia tortured 12 men accused of being gay and threatened them with death. In Derna, Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in April 2015, and Islamic State fighters killed men accused of homosexuality in the territory they held; a young man in Derna was targeted by local Islamists in November 2014 for effeminate dress and "contemporary" clothes.

Reporting from 2015 concluded that the situation for homosexuals in Libya was deteriorating as militias controlled territory, with information in Derna reaching the outside world only through the mosque. A 2010 French asylum case involved a Libyan girl who, after stating online that she was gay, was jailed, raped and returned to her family for a forced marriage; the account gives no age, schooling or student status.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement recorded in these sources rests heavily on non-state actors. The documented incidents cluster in 2012, 2014 and 2015, periods in which militias and armed groups held territory and the coercive power of the state was fragmented, so the practical risk came from patrol points, checkpoints and local commanders rather than from a routine court process.

Criminalisation reaches presentation as well as conduct. Because Cairo 52 treats transition itself, social and medical alike, as caught by the indecent-acts provisions, a trans visitor may be questioned over dress, documents and attempts to obtain care rather than over any partnered activity.

The Guardian's guide places Libya within a regional group of states where homosexuality carries imprisonment and specific terms differ by country, which places Libya's five-year ceiling for indecent acts alongside differing penalties elsewhere rather than at either extreme.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot obtain legal gender recognition, and official identity documents cannot be altered to reflect a person's gender. Any transition undertaken in the country, social or medical, stands exposed to the indecent-acts and illicit-intercourse provisions of the Penal Code.

Religious rulings have declared gender-affirming medical steps impermissible, which constrains both the supply of and the ability to seek such care without attracting attention.

There is no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing or services, and same-sex relationships enjoy no legal recognition. LGBTI organisations cannot register, which removes the ordinary route to advocacy, service provision and collective complaint.

People accused of homosexual acts have faced torture and summary execution at the hands of militias and Islamist groups, including the 12 men detained by a militia in 2012 and the three young men killed in Derna in April 2015. Arrest or accusation on these grounds carries a real risk of violence outside any formal sentence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2010 French asylum account gives no age for the Libyan girl involved, no schooling or student status, and no information on her subsequent whereabouts; the case is reported second-hand and its details are unresolved.

Whether the indecent-acts provisions have been charged specifically against trans defendants, as distinct from men who have sex with men, is not sourced in this inventory. Cairo 52's finding of de-facto criminalisation is a review conclusion rather than a reported prosecution.

The violence documentation from Derna relies on information channels that at the time passed only through the mosque, so casualty counts and the identities of those killed there cannot be independently confirmed from these sources.

Current enforcement practice is only partly covered: the Outright International overview is dated 12 March 2026, but the incidents of torture and execution are drawn from 2012 to 2015 reporting, and no source in this inventory records a post-2016 case of prosecution or of violence against a trans visitor.
